variants.text:
Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

My dad gave me one piece of advice about sex: before you do it, ask each other whether you would want to raise children together and whether you're ready. That question started this whole article. I still think it's the best advice in it for people living in permissive cultures, where sex has been separated from the assumption that a baby and a life together may follow. In more traditional cultures, that part may already be assumed, which is why the rest of this article can't just be my dad's advice.

If you can really talk about raising children together, most of the other important questions come up on their own. What kind of life do I want? What kind of life do you want? What would we want for a child? What would sex mean between us?

I still want to talk about the sex itself before we're naked, because that's a terrible time to discover that one of us has been afraid to say what we actually want. What makes your body relax and open? Is there anything kinky you need to be able to say out loud? What has your past made you want, or made you avoid? What just doesn't work?

I may not know all my answers either. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you” is a perfectly good answer. And sex doesn't even have to be for the same thing every time. One day it may mainly be bonding, another day play; sometimes it feels sacred, and sometimes it may just be how you come down from a bad day.

Our sex drives aren't going to stay perfectly matched forever. For some stretch, one of us will want more, less, or something different, and that's one of the easiest ways for quiet resentment to start growing. I'd rather talk while neither person is already hurt: what are we going to do when that happens? We can't solve it in advance, but at least we'll have somewhere to begin.

Then there's the harder test: can I still say what I want once we're naked if I think she'll be disappointed? If not, we're both just hoping sex will sort out what neither of us wanted to say. Bodies fitting isn't enough. Can we stay honest while we're completely exposed?

Talking about all of this before our clothes come off already practices some of the trust and willingness to be seen that making love needs. It also naturally slows sex down. If we can't have the conversation at all, that's a red flag for the relationship's chances of success.

The problem is when the role takes over the relationship. She can be my little girl sometimes without becoming my child. She still has to remain responsible for her life and keep reparenting herself.

It can run the other way too. If I expect her to regulate me, soothe every wound, organize my life, and keep me functional, then I’ve made her Mom.

All three women eventually told me they felt like my patient, and I could see why. I was the person they brought almost every medical, mental-health, and practical problem to:

“I’m sick. What should I take?”

“I’m sad. What should I do?”

Of course I was going to help. If every time one of them felt sick I answered, “I’m not your doctor or therapist,” that would have been cold. But after enough of those conversations, I understood why they used the word patient.

Key at first asked me innocently, "Can you be my guru?" I told her, “I’m not anyone's guru, but we can learn from each other.” A few months later, she was telling me she was much more spiritually advanced than me. I asked, “Do you recall asking me to be your guru?” She said, "Wow, I must have been really confused back then!"

I also have to admit, I can become condescending when somebody stops taking responsibility for their behavior. I find that intolerable. If someone says, “I feel like your patient,” both people need to look at their roles.
